Toothy flathead (Platycephalus aurimaculatus) is a relatively small-bodied platycephalid that reaches an ultimate total length of 55 cm [Li = 55 cm], though individuals exceeding 50 cm are uncommon in coastal trawl surveys. Field measurements indicate that sexual maturation begins when fish attain approximately 30 cm [Lp = approximately 30 cm] total length, a threshold that corresponds with the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both sexes. The species is iteroparous, and mature individuals spawn multiple times during the austral summer months. Larval development proceeds rapidly under controlled conditions; newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from demersal eggs after an incubation period of 10 days [ab = 10 days] when held at a stable water temperature of 16.4 °C [T = 16.4 °C]. These prolarvae are lecithotrophic and remain non-feeding until yolk absorption is complete, after which exogenous feeding commences. The relatively short embryonic phase is consistent with the fast life-history strategy observed in other temperate platycephalids.

Neonatal body mass is remarkably low, with each newly emerged prolarva weighing just 0.000065 g [Wwb = 0.000065 g] based on an average egg diameter of 0.5 millimeters. This minute wet weight at birth reflects the small pelagic egg size characteristic of the genus and imposes a substantial energetic challenge during the early larval period, as the endotrophic larva must rapidly develop functional feeding structures before endogenous reserves are exhausted. The species exhibits a steep growth trajectory during the first few months post-settlement, with juveniles quickly reaching sizes that reduce vulnerability to gape-limited predators. Comparative data from related flathead species suggest that the combination of small egg size and rapid larval development may represent an adaptation to seasonally productive coastal environments where planktonic food resources are abundant but temporally variable. The trade-off between egg size and fecundity is evident in this species.

Adult body mass is strongly correlated with length, and the largest recorded individuals attain an ultimate wet weight of 1953 grams [Wwi = 1953 grams], although most captured adults weigh between 800 and 1500 grams depending on local prey availability and density-dependent growth regulation. This asymptotic mass is achieved over several years of sustained feeding on benthic crustaceans and small teleosts. The weight-length relationship in P. aurimaculatus follows a typical positive allometric pattern, with heavier fish exhibiting disproportionately greater girth relative to length, a common feature among demersal ambush predators. Seasonal variation in body condition is pronounced, with peak masses recorded during late summer following the period of highest prey abundance. The 1953 gram [Wwi = 1953 gram] maximum represents a substantial investment in somatic tissue that supports both the energetic demands of reproduction and the capacity to endure periods of reduced foraging success during winter months.

Maximum longevity in this species has been estimated from otolith increment analysis, with the oldest documented individual reaching an age of 18 years [am = 18 years] under natural environmental conditions at 16.4 °C [T = 16.4 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a fish of its body size reflects a life-history strategy that balances moderate annual reproductive output against sustained adult survival. The age structure of wild populations typically comprises multiple year-classes, indicating consistent recruitment across years despite interannual variability in oceanographic conditions. Senescence is evident in the oldest age classes, with reduced condition factor and lower fecundity observed in fish beyond 15 years. The 18-year (18 years) [am = 18 years] lifespan permits multiple reproductive episodes over the adult lifetime, a classic iteroparous pattern that buffers the population against occasional recruitment failures at a temperature of 16.4 °C [T = 16.4 °C].

The total length at puberty of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] corresponds roughly to an age of three to four years in most populations, though growth rates vary considerably with local temperature and food supply. At this size, individuals have typically completed the transition from a strictly piscivorous juvenile diet to the broader benthic carnivory characteristic of adults. Gonadal development proceeds during the cooler months, with spawning activity peaking in late spring when water temperatures rise above 15 °C. The ecological role of P. aurimaculatus as a mesopredator in soft-sediment habitats is reinforced by its relatively early attainment of sexual maturity, which ensures that reproductive output begins well before the cessation of somatic growth. Field studies indicate that larger females contribute disproportionately to total egg production, highlighting the importance of protecting older, larger individuals within the population to maintain reproductive resilience.
